steps.say: total = 0 runs at the top of the file, so total is a global name.
Inside the call, n is 5. This call has its own local names.
This line assigns to total, so inside add, total is a new local name. Python reads that local before it has a value.
steps.error_label: UnboundLocalError: local variable 'total' referenced before assignment

steps.say: Fix: pass total in and return the new value: def add(total, n): return total + n, then total = add(total, 5).

pages.title: Where variables live
paragraphs: Every name in a Python program has a home. The home decides which parts of your code are allowed to see it.
A name you create at the top of the file is global, so every function can read it. A name a function assigns to is local, and it disappears when that call finishes.

key_term.definition: the region of code where a name can be used.

pages.title: Pass in, return out
paragraphs: Assigning to a name inside a function makes a new local name, even if a global one has the same name.
The safe way to change a value is to pass it in and return the new one. The caller stores what comes back.

key_term.definition: a name created inside a function; it only exists while that call runs.

transcript: Every name in a program lives somewhere.
Names made at the top of the file are global, and every function can read them.
Names a function assigns to are local, and they vanish when the call ends.
If a function assigns to total, Python treats total as local inside it.
Reading that local before it has a value raises UnboundLocalError.
So pass values in, return the result, and let the caller keep it.
